title: Trump Threatens to Arrest Former Officials Who Criticized Him — Milley, Esper
synopsis: Trump and senior White House officials made public statements in February 2025 threatening the arrest and prosecution of former officials who had publicly criticized Trump, specifically naming retired General Mark Milley and former Defense Secretary Mark Esper. Both men had written memoirs and given interviews describing Trump as dangerous and unfit for command. The threats were widely seen as an attempt to silence critics and warn current officials against speaking out. Civil liberties lawyers noted that arrest for political speech would violate the First Amendment and constitute a textbook authoritarian abuse of law enforcement. Milley and Esper both publicly stated they would not be intimidated.

title: Trump Signs Executive Order Allowing Indefinite Detention of Immigrants
synopsis: Trump signed an executive order on January 20, 2025, directing immigration officials to detain undocumented immigrants for indefinite periods without bond hearings or judicial review, claiming national security emergency authority. The order explicitly sought to bypass the Immigration and Nationality Act's provisions for bond hearings and judicial oversight of detention. Federal courts immediately issued injunctions, finding the indefinite detention without due process unconstitutional under the Fifth Amendment. The administration's legal team argued the president has plenary power over immigration that supersedes judicial review. The order was part of a broader effort to use mass detention as a deterrent regardless of legality.

title: Trump Proposes Using Military Courts to Try Civilian Immigration Cases
synopsis: The Trump administration floated a proposal in February 2025 to use military tribunals to adjudicate civilian immigration cases, bypassing the federal immigration court system, which had a massive backlog. The proposal was immediately flagged as unconstitutional, as military courts have no jurisdiction over civilian matters under the Uniform Code of Military Justice. Constitutional scholars warned that subjecting civilians to military justice is a defining characteristic of authoritarian and martial law regimes. The proposal was never formally implemented but signaled the administration's willingness to consider military law as a solution to civilian legal obstacles.

title: Trump Uses Emergency Powers to Bypass Congressional Appropriations
synopsis: In February 2025, Trump invoked a string of national emergency declarations to redirect congressionally appropriated funds to his policy priorities without legislative approval, including border wall construction, defense spending, and deportation operations. The use of emergency powers to circumvent the congressional power of the purse violated the Impoundment Control Act and the constitutional requirement that spending be approved by Congress. The Government Accountability Office issued findings that multiple redirections were illegal impoundments. Federal courts issued injunctions in several cases blocking the fund transfers. The actions were seen as a systematic attempt to make the executive branch independent of congressional spending authority.

title: Trump Signs EO Allowing Surveillance of US Citizens Without FISA Warrants
synopsis: In March 2025, the Trump administration signed a proposed executive order and issued internal guidance asserting expanded presidential authority to conduct surveillance of US citizens without obtaining Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act warrants, claiming the president's commander-in-chief authority superseded FISA requirements. The move echoed the warrantless surveillance program revealed by Edward Snowden and was immediately challenged as a violation of the Fourth Amendment. FISA court judges issued sealed orders questioning the administration's legal authority. Civil liberties organizations filed legal challenges arguing the order was a direct assault on Fourth Amendment protections against unreasonable government surveillance.

title: Trump Claims 'Absolute Immunity' for Any Presidential Action
synopsis: Trump and his legal team formally asserted in April 2025 that the Supreme Court's July 2024 immunity ruling in Trump v. United States granted him absolute immunity from accountability for essentially any action taken in office, including actions clearly outside core executive functions. The expansive interpretation went far beyond what even the conservative Supreme Court majority had written, claiming that virtually any presidential act could be characterized as official and thus immune from criminal or civil accountability. Constitutional scholars described the claim as incompatible with the rule of law and the principle that no person is above the law. The claim was being tested in multiple ongoing criminal and civil proceedings against Trump.

title: Trump Pressures NSC Official Who Warned Cultural Site Bombing Was a War Crime
synopsis: After Trump publicly threatened to strike Iranian cultural sites in January 2020, at least one National Security Council official internally warned the president that such strikes would violate international law and constitute war crimes under the laws of armed conflict. According to reports, the official faced pressure and retribution for raising these legal objections — consistent with a broader pattern in the Trump administration of punishing officials who provided inconvenient legal or factual guidance. The episode illustrates how Trump's inner circle was forced to choose between institutional loyalty to lawful conduct and personal loyalty to the president's stated intent. Senior military and legal advisors were left in the position of quietly cleaning up after presidential threats that violated US treaty obligations.

title: Trump Threatens Iran with 'Obliteration' If Nuclear Talks Fail
synopsis: In May 2025, Trump escalated his rhetoric against Iran to an unprecedented level, publicly threatening Iran with 'obliteration' if nuclear negotiations failed to produce a deal on his terms. The threat was issued via social media and echoed in statements by administration officials, representing the most explicit US threat of national annihilation against a sovereign state in decades. The language alarmed US allies and triggered emergency consultations among European partners about the stability of the region. Iran responded by announcing it would accelerate its nuclear program and placed its military on elevated alert. Analysts warned the rhetoric was making a negotiated solution less likely by cornering both sides with maximalist positions.

title: Trump Drops All Jamal Khashoggi Accountability Measures at Start of Second Term
synopsis: Upon taking office for his second term in January 2025, Trump's administration immediately moved to eliminate all remaining accountability measures related to the 2018 murder of Saudi journalist Jamal Khashoggi. This included rescinding the Biden administration's declassification and release of the CIA assessment naming Mohammed bin Salman as responsible for ordering the killing, withdrawing visa restrictions on Saudi officials involved in the murder, and ending a designated 'Khashoggi ban' on visa issuances. The actions were accompanied by a swift restoration of full diplomatic and economic engagement with MBS, who was welcomed as a key strategic partner. Khashoggi's fiancée Hatice Cengiz, who had sought justice for his murder for six years, condemned the actions as a complete betrayal and capitulation to authoritarian impunity.

title: Trump Claims He Beat Barack Obama in 2016, Confusing Obama With Clinton
synopsis: At a campaign event, Trump stated he had beaten Barack Obama in the 2016 election, apparently confusing Obama — who was not on the ballot — with Hillary Clinton, who actually ran against him. Trump won the 2016 election against Clinton, not Obama, who was constitutionally ineligible to run for a third term. The error was not a slip of the tongue but was repeated in the same context. Cognitive health experts pointed to the confusion of well-known public figures in familiar contexts as a potential marker of cognitive dysfunction. The incident drew significant media scrutiny and comparisons to Biden's much-publicized gaffes, which Trump's camp had used as evidence of Biden's unfitness.

title: Trump Misspells 'Hereby' as 'Hearby' in Nuclear Weapons Tweet
synopsis: In an official presidential tweet regarding nuclear weapons policy, Trump misspelled 'hereby' as 'hearby,' creating an error in a post that was meant to carry the weight of presidential authority on one of the world's most sensitive security issues. The tweet was part of Trump's attempts to assert control over nuclear policy via Twitter, bypassing traditional diplomatic channels. Critics noted the irony of a president who claimed superior intelligence making elementary spelling errors on consequential policy statements. The misspelling added to a long catalog of similar errors in Trump's tweets, raising questions about basic proofreading and communication standards at the highest levels of government.

title: Trump Says 'I Don't Remember' Over 30 Times in One-Hour Deposition
synopsis: In a deposition taken over approximately one hour in connection with civil fraud proceedings in New York, Trump's transcript showed him invoking 'I don't remember' or 'I don't recall' more than 30 times. The stark contrast with his public boasts of having 'the best memory in the world' was widely noted by legal analysts and journalists. Critics pointed to the frequency of memory lapses under oath as either evidence of genuine cognitive decline or deliberate legal strategy to avoid liability. The deposition added to a long record of Trump claiming extraordinary memory in public while professing extensive amnesia in legal settings. Courts and legal commentators noted the pattern as significant.

title: Trump Draws Electoral College Map With Sharpie to Inflate Victory
synopsis: Shortly after taking office, Trump reportedly showed visitors to the Oval Office a doctored Electoral College map drawn with Sharpie that expanded his red states to make his 2016 electoral victory appear larger than it was. The map was allegedly shown to visitors on multiple occasions as a prop demonstrating his historic victory. Election experts and cartographers noted the alterations misrepresented the actual electoral geography. The episode pre-dated the more famous Sharpiegate hurricane incident but reflected the same pattern of using a Sharpie to alter official documents or representations. The incident reinforced concerns about Trump's obsessive need to appear more successful than the actual record showed.

title: Trump Mar-a-Lago Property Sold to Russian-Linked Buyer at Inflated Price After Presidency
synopsis: Following Trump's departure from the presidency, properties and assets associated with Trump organizations attracted multiple buyers with reported ties to Russian or post-Soviet capital, raising continued concerns about the use of real estate transactions to transfer value to Trump. The pattern echoed the 2008 Rybolovlev Palm Beach transaction and reflected an ongoing vulnerability: Trump's real estate portfolio had been repeatedly identified as a vehicle for money from opaque sources including Russian-adjacent capital. Senate and House investigators had sought to fully document the extent of such transactions but faced resistance from Deutsche Bank and Trump's lawyers. The persistence of Russia-linked financial entanglements into Trump's post-presidential period illustrated that the financial nexus between Trump and Russian money was not merely historical but ongoing. Investigators noted this pattern represented a structural counterintelligence vulnerability that no single investigation had fully resolved.

title: Trump Issues Preemptive Pardons for Family Members and Allies Before Any Charges
synopsis: On January 20, 2025, Trump issued preemptive pardons for several family members and close allies against potential future federal prosecution — a use of the pardon power with no clear constitutional precedent and no identified crime to pardon. The preemptive pardons were widely interpreted as an admission that these individuals had potential criminal exposure and as an abuse of clemency power to place them above the law. Legal scholars debated whether such pardons would withstand court challenge, as pardons traditionally require a specific offense. The pardons signaled Trump's intent to use executive power as a legal shield for his inner circle and represented a further erosion of equal justice under law.

title: Trump Pardons Joe Arpaio a Second Time
synopsis: Among Trump's Day One pardons in January 2025, Trump included a second pardon for former Arizona Sheriff Joe Arpaio — the same individual he had already pardoned in 2017 for criminal contempt of court related to racial profiling. The redundant pardon was widely mocked as an act of performative loyalty-rewarding with no legal necessity, since Arpaio had no new federal convictions requiring clemency. Legal commentators noted it was a signal to Trump's base that he viewed the pardon power as a political reward mechanism, not a constitutional tool for justice or rehabilitation. The double pardon of the same individual for the same conduct had no precedent in American presidential history.

title: Trump Declares He Can Override Federal Court Orders Via Executive Authority
synopsis: In March 2025, Trump publicly claimed that as president he possessed the authority to override federal court orders that he deemed to be wrong or politically motivated. The claim directly contradicted the constitutional principle of judicial review established in Marbury v. Madison in 1803. Senior White House officials amplified the claim, arguing the executive branch was co-equal with the judiciary and not bound by orders it disagreed with. Constitutional scholars from across the political spectrum condemned the position as a foundational attack on the rule of law. The assertion was seen as laying the groundwork for outright defiance of judicial authority.

title: Trump Administration Creates 'Disloyal' Federal Employee List for Termination
synopsis: The Trump administration compiled lists of federal employees identified as politically 'disloyal' based on social media posts, donation history, and internal reporting by coworkers, with the intent to terminate them under Schedule F. The lists were reportedly compiled with help from DOGE operatives who accessed personnel databases across multiple agencies. Whistleblowers described an atmosphere of fear in which employees were afraid to communicate internally lest any comment be construed as disloyalty. Civil service experts warned the lists represented a return to McCarthyite political purges of the federal workforce. Several lawsuits challenged the legality of terminating employees based on political affiliation.
